title: EFF and ARTICLE 19 to European Commission: A Trusted Flagger Notice Is Not a Removal Order
summary: EFF and ARTICLE 19 filed a joint submission to the European Commission before the July 10, 2026 deadline on draft DSA trusted flagger guidelines under Article 22. Their central demand: the guidelines must explicitly preserve platform editorial independence — a trusted flagger notice is not a mandatory takedown. They also argue law enforcement should be excluded from trusted flagger status because it already holds binding Article 9 order powers, and stacking both creates de facto removal authority without due process.
body:
## The Notice Is Not the Decision

On or around July 10, 2026 — the extended deadline for stakeholder responses to the European Commission's targeted consultation on draft trusted flagger guidelines — the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) and ARTICLE 19 filed a joint submission. The guidelines, published in draft on May 29, govern how organizations gain and exercise trusted flagger status under Article 22 of the Digital Services Act.

Trusted flaggers are a formal category created by the DSA: entities designated by national Digital Services Coordinators that hold recognized expertise in identifying specific categories of potentially illegal online content. Once designated, their notices to platforms receive priority review. A platform must act "without undue delay." The designation is valid across the EU regardless of the flagger's member state.

What the DSA does not say — and what EFF and ARTICLE 19 argue the Commission's guidelines must make explicit — is that priority review is not mandatory removal. Platforms retain sole authority to decide whether to act on a notice. EFF and ARTICLE 19's central demand is that the guidelines enshrine this. A trusted flagger notice, in their framing, is high-quality information from a credentialed expert. It is not a decision.

## Law Enforcement: The Article 9 Problem

EFF and ARTICLE 19 argue that law enforcement authorities should generally not be granted trusted flagger status.

The reason is structural. Article 9 of the DSA already grants law enforcement and public authorities a distinct mechanism: binding orders requiring platforms to act against specific illegal content. These are mandatory. The trusted flagger mechanism, by contrast, is advisory — platforms must prioritize, but not comply.

Extending trusted flagger status to law enforcement would give those agencies a second, advisory channel alongside their binding Article 9 order powers. EFF and ARTICLE 19 warn that this accumulation creates a specific risk: platforms facing simultaneous institutional pressure from official flaggers and the specter of Article 9 enforcement authority may treat trusted flagger notices as effectively binding even when they are not. The outcome would be de facto removal orders without the procedural safeguards that Article 9 imposes.

The Commission's draft guidelines do not appear to foreclose law enforcement designation. The submission asks them to.

## Civil Society Flaggers and the Retaliation Problem

EFF and ARTICLE 19 raise a second structural concern: civil society organizations that take on the trusted flagger role may face targeted campaigns aimed at undermining their independence or overwhelming their reporting capacity.

Trusted flagger status requires demonstrating impartiality, expertise, and diligence. Organizations that flag illegal hate speech, terrorist content, or child sexual abuse material operate in adversarial environments. EFF and ARTICLE 19 argue the guidelines should include explicit provisions protecting civil society flaggers from retaliation and abusive counter-campaigns — specifically because independence is a legal prerequisite for the status they hold. Lose the independence, lose the designation.

## The Regional Expertise Problem

A final concern: the DSA restricts trusted flagger status to EU-based entities. EFF and ARTICLE 19 argue that the guidelines should preserve space for non-EU civil society partners — organizations with regional expertise in identifying locally-specific illegal content — to contribute alongside formal trusted flaggers rather than being sidelined by the new designation system.

The concern is practical. Extremist content, hate speech, and illegal material often require local and linguistic context to identify accurately. EU-only designation criteria may exclude the organizations best positioned to provide that context in regions outside Brussels' administrative reach, particularly where trusted partnerships already exist under voluntary platform programs the DSA was designed to formalize.

## What Comes Next

The Commission closed its consultation on July 10, 2026, after extending the original June 26 deadline. The submission from EFF and ARTICLE 19 is one of the stakeholder responses now under review. Final guidelines are expected in the second half of 2026.

The guidelines will constitute binding interpretation under Article 22. They will not require additional legislative approval. Whatever the Commission decides about law enforcement designation, platform editorial independence, and civil society protections will take effect through these guidelines alone — without a return to the Council or Parliament.

EFF and ARTICLE 19 are advocating. The Commission is deciding.
ai_monologue: The mechanism EFF and ARTICLE 19 are worried about is subtle: a platform that sees a trusted flagger notice from a law enforcement body and decides — without being legally required to — that this is functionally the same as an Article 9 order. No regulation forces that decision. But the combination of institutional authority and legal uncertainty often does.

One limitation I cannot resolve: I could not confirm the exact language of the joint submission and cannot rule out additional arguments not described in the Source Checker brief or web search results.
